name: Graceful Degradation
intent: Keep the core function working when a part fails or is too slow, by serving a reduced experience instead of failing the whole request.
scenario: A product page needs the product service (critical) plus reviews, recommendations, inventory and personalisation (optional). Recommendations starts taking 2 seconds per call. Without a plan, every product page takes 2 seconds or errors; with one, the page loads in about 300 ms with generic bestsellers where the recommendations were.
problem: A page that depends on five services is only as reliable as all five together: at 99.9% each, the page is about 99.5% available, and it is as slow as the slowest one. Most of those services are decoration. Treating every dependency as mandatory turns a failure of the least important feature into an outage of the most important page.

howItWorks.title: Classify every dependency: critical or optional
howItWorks.text: Ask of each call: if it is gone, is the request still worth answering? The product service is critical, because the page is about the product. Reviews, recommendations, inventory badges and personalisation are optional. Write the classification down in code, one place, not scattered across handlers. Be strict about what counts as critical: every dependency you promote to critical multiplies the ways the page can fail.

howItWorks.title: Give optional calls their own short timeout
howItWorks.text: Call dependencies in parallel and give optional ones a budget a fraction of the page's: 200 to 500 ms against a 2 s critical timeout is typical. The page latency is the slowest call you wait for, so a slow optional call with a long timeout drags the whole page down (see timeouts-and-deadlines). A circuit breaker on each optional dependency skips the call entirely once it is known to be failing.

howItWorks.title: Choose a fallback for each optional part
howItWorks.text: In order of fidelity: serve the last cached value, even if stale (stale-if-error: reviews from yesterday); use a default or generic answer (bestsellers instead of personalised recommendations, the logged-out view when personalisation is down); show a simplified or static version; or hide the widget. The fallback must be cheap and independent: a local cache or a constant, never another call to a busy system.

howItWorks.title: Fail open or fail closed, per feature
howItWorks.text: Fail open means that when the check or feature is unavailable, the request proceeds without it. A recommendations box fails open. Fail closed means that it is refused. An authorization check, a fraud decision on a payment and a rate limit protecting a fragile backend fail closed, because proceeding would be worse than the error. Decide this per dependency, in advance, not during the incident.

howItWorks.title: Add load-shedding switches
howItWorks.text: A kill switch (a feature flag, see feature-flags) lets an operator turn off an expensive optional feature by hand or automatically under load: no recommendations during a traffic peak, so the CPU goes to the checkout path. Return a partial response with a marker of which parts are missing, so clients can render the rest.

howItWorks.title: Make degradation visible, and test it
howItWorks.text: Emit a counter per degraded part and a response header or banner, and alert when the degraded share passes a threshold such as 5%. Exercise every fallback regularly (fault injection, game days, a staging switch that fails each dependency in turn), because a fallback that has never run is the one that crashes the first time you need it.

pros: The core function survives the failure of its decorations, so most users never notice an incident
Latency stays bounded: optional calls cannot drag the page past their timeout
Turns a binary outage into a gradient, which buys time to fix things without a full incident
Cheap to start: a timeout, a try/catch and a default value already give most of the benefit
cons: Every fallback is more code, more states and more test cases to maintain
Stale or generic data can be wrong: a cached 'in stock' can sell an item that has run out
Degradation can hide a real outage if nothing measures it
Needs product decisions: someone must agree what 'good enough' looks like, which is not an engineering call alone
whenToUse: Pages and APIs that aggregate many backends of unequal importance
Features that are nice to have, such as recommendations, ads, personalisation, social proof or analytics
Any dependency with a known tail latency (a small share of calls that are very slow) or a lower SLO (service level objective, the availability target) than the function that calls it
whenNotToUse: Operations where a wrong or stale answer is worse than none: payments, authorization, inventory reservation at checkout, anything that moves money or grants access (fail closed instead)
When the 'optional' part is the point of the product: a search page with search down has nothing to degrade to
Features too small or too stable to justify a second code path that will rot
pitfalls: Silent fallbacks: the page looks fine, the dashboard is green, and recommendations have been generic for three weeks because nothing counted it
Fallbacks that were never exercised: the cache key changed, the default value no longer parses, and the first real failure crashes the fallback path too

A fallback that overloads another system: on a cache miss every request falls back to the primary database, which turns a reviews outage into a database outage. Fallbacks must be cheaper than the call they replace
Optional timeouts set too long (or inherited from a library default of 30 s), so the page waits anyway and the fallback never gets a chance
Marking something critical 'in case', which makes a failure in a decorative feature a full outage
Serving stale data forever: a stale-if-error copy needs a maximum age (hours, not weeks) and a visible 'as of' for data users act on, such as prices and stock
Fail-open on a security or safety check because it was easy to wrap in a try/catch that returns the default

roles.label: Page service
roles.description: Fans out to dependencies, applies per-call timeouts and fallbacks, and decides full, degraded or error.

roles.label: Critical dependency
roles.description: Without it the request is not worth answering. Its failure fails the page.

roles.label: Optional dependency
roles.description: Enhances the page. Its failure or slowness is absorbed by a fallback or by hiding the part.

roles.label: Fallback source
roles.description: A stale cache, a default or a generic ranking that costs almost nothing to read.

quiz.question: A product page must answer in 500 ms. It calls the product service (critical) and a recommendations service (optional). Recommendations now take 2 seconds, and the HTTP client uses its default 30 second timeout. What is the best change?
options: Give recommendations a 200 ms timeout, and show cached bestsellers when it expires.
Raise the page timeout to 3 seconds, so that the recommendations have enough time to finish.
Retry recommendations three times, so that at least one of the calls is likely to be fast.
Call recommendations first, and call the product service only if recommendations succeed.
quiz.explanation: An optional dependency needs its own short budget and a cheap fallback, so the page stays near its target. Retries and a longer page timeout both make users wait for something decorative, and making the critical service wait on recommendations adds a new way to fail.

quiz.question: A checkout calls a fraud-scoring service that is now down. An engineer wraps the call in try/catch that returns approved, calling it graceful degradation, so payments keep flowing. Compliance says every payment must be screened before it is taken. What is the better design?
options: Reuse the last fraud score seen for that customer, for up to 24 hours after it was computed.
Keep returning approved, but log each case so that analysts can review them afterwards.
Fail closed: refuse or hold the payment, since a wrong approval costs more than a delay.
Return approved only for orders under a fixed amount, and run the same check for every other order.
quiz.explanation: A check that protects money or access should fail closed, because proceeding without it can cost more than the error. The remaining options still approve payments that were never screened (an old score does not describe this payment), which is the same risk in smaller or later form.

quiz.question: A product page shows reviews from a cache. On a cache miss, the fallback is to read reviews straight from the primary database. When the reviews service fails, the cache empties and the main database falls over. What should change?
options: Increase the primary database size so that it can absorb the extra read load without falling over.
Retry the reviews service more often, with backoff, before the fallback path is used at all.
Add a second database call as a backup in case the fallback path to the first one fails.
Use a cheap independent fallback such as a stale copy with a maximum age, else hide the widget.
quiz.explanation: A fallback must be cheaper than the call it replaces and must not depend on a busy shared system. Pointing it at the primary database turns a decorative outage into a core outage. More retries add load, bigger hardware only moves the limit, and a second database call is one more thing that fails under the same load.
